title: Interfaces vs Abstract Classes
summary: Two ways to leave gaps for subclasses to fill. Learn when a pure contract beats a shared base class.

blocks.markdown:
An **interface** is a pure contract — method signatures only, no state, no code. An **abstract class** is a partial class — it can hold state and shared code, but can't be instantiated on its own.

- Both exist so a concrete class fills in the missing pieces.
- Interface answers **"what can you do?"**; abstract class answers **"what are you, mostly?"**
- A class can implement many interfaces but extend only one class.

An **interface** lists method **signatures** (name, parameters, return type) with no bodies and no fields. It promises *what* a class can do, never *how*.

- No **state** — an interface can't store data of its own.
- Any class, unrelated to any other, can implement it if it supplies the methods.
- Implementing one is a promise: "I support this behavior."

An **abstract class** can hold **state** (fields) and a **partial implementation** — some methods fully written, others left as **abstract methods** (signature only, body supplied by subclasses).

- It **can't be instantiated** directly — you can never write `new Shape()` if `Shape` is abstract.
- Subclasses inherit its state and finished methods for free, and must fill in the abstract ones.
- Best for things that are genuinely the *same kind of thing* underneath.

The core split, side by side.

| | Interface | Abstract class |
|---|---|---|
| State | None | Yes, fields allowed |
| Implementation | None (or default methods) | Partial — mix of done and abstract |
| Multiple use | A class implements many | A class extends only one |

Interface = contract only. Abstract class = shared foundation plus contract.

blocks.subTitle: An interface
blocks.markdown:
```text
// pure contract — signatures only, no state
interface Flyable:
    method fly()

interface Swimmable:
    method swim()
```

blocks.subTitle: An abstract class
blocks.markdown:
```text
// partial implementation — has state + some finished methods
abstract class Bird:
    name              // state, shared by all birds

    constructor(name):
        this.name = name

    method describe():           // fully implemented, inherited as-is
        print(this.name + " is a bird")

    abstract method makeSound()  // no body — subclass must supply it
```

blocks.subTitle: A concrete class using both
blocks.markdown:
```text
// extends one abstract class, implements two interfaces
class Duck extends Bird implements Flyable, Swimmable:

    constructor(name):
        super(name)          // reuse Bird's constructor

    method makeSound():      // fills the abstract gap
        print(this.name + " says Quack")

    method fly():             // fills the Flyable contract
        print(this.name + " flies low over the pond")

    method swim():            // fills the Swimmable contract
        print(this.name + " paddles across the pond")

d = new Duck("Donald")
d.describe()    // Donald is a bird       (inherited, unchanged)
d.makeSound()   // Donald says Quack      (abstract method filled in)
d.fly()         // Donald flies low over the pond
d.swim()        // Donald paddles across the pond
```

One base class for shared "bird-ness"; two interfaces for unrelated capabilities.

Choose by what you're modeling.

- **Interface** — a **"can-do"** capability shared by otherwise unrelated types. A `Car` and a `Duck` can both be `Movable`, nothing else in common.
- **Abstract class** — a shared base plus real common code. All `Bird` subclasses genuinely *are* birds and share `name` and `describe()`.
- Mixing both, like `Duck` above, is normal and often the best fit.

**"Program to an interface, not an implementation"** means code should depend on the contract (what a type promises) rather than one concrete class (how it's built).

- Write `Flyable bird`, not `Duck bird` — your code no longer cares which bird it is.
- Swapping in a `Sparrow` or a mock for tests needs **zero changes** to the calling code.
- This is what makes systems open to new types without editing old code. See [polymorphism](polymorphism), [solid-principles](solid-principles).

Modern languages (Java 8+, C# 8+) allow **default methods** — an interface method with a body, used when an implementer doesn't override it.

- Lets you add a new method to an interface without breaking every existing implementer.
- Still no state — a default method can only use what's passed in or other interface methods, not fields.
- Doesn't turn an interface into an abstract class; it just softens the "no code" rule.

Common mistakes:

- **"Abstract class = interface with extra steps."** No — state and single inheritance make them fit different problems, not interchangeable syntax.
- **Forcing shared code through an interface.** Default methods help, but an interface still can't hold state; don't stretch it into a base class.
- **One giant abstract base for everything.** If subclasses share little, you're forcing a false "is-a" relationship — prefer smaller interfaces.

blocks.subTitle: Key differences
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What's the difference between an interface and an abstract class?**

An interface is a pure contract — signatures only, no state, and a class can implement several. An abstract class can hold state and partially-finished code, but a class can extend only one. Interfaces define *what*; abstract classes can also define *how*, partially.

blocks.subTitle: Choosing between them
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: When would you choose an abstract class over an interface?**

When subclasses genuinely share state or common code and you'd otherwise duplicate it everywhere. Use an interface when unrelated types just need to promise the same capability, with nothing else in common.

blocks.subTitle: Multiple interfaces vs multiple classes
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Can a class implement multiple interfaces? Extend multiple classes?**

Yes to interfaces — most languages allow implementing any number, since there's no state to conflict. No to classes in Java/C#-style languages — extending two base classes risks clashing inherited state, so only single inheritance is allowed there.

blocks.subTitle: Program to an interface
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What does "program to an interface, not an implementation" mean?**

Depend on the contract type in your code, not a specific concrete class. A variable typed as `Flyable` accepts any flyer; swapping the real class underneath needs no change to the code that uses it.

blocks.subTitle: Can an interface have state
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Can an interface hold state or a constructor?**

No. An interface has no fields and no constructor — only method signatures, plus optional default method bodies in modern languages. Any state needed must live in the implementing class.

blocks.subTitle: Why can't you instantiate an abstract class
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why can't you instantiate an abstract class directly?**

Because it's incomplete by design — it has at least one abstract method with no body. Creating an instance would leave a method callable with nothing to run, so the language blocks it until a concrete subclass fills every gap.
